brand.title: IQVIA (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to CTFS for TechIQ

questions.question: What does CTFS stand for?
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly! CTFS is IQVIA's Clinical Trial Financial Suite, designed to bring major financial activities of a clinical trial into one connected experience.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. CTFS stands for Clinical Trial Financial Suite, which is IQVIA's platform for unifying financial operations across clinical trials. Take another look at Slide 1.

questions.question: Since 2019, by what percentage has the number of trial sites grown?
questions.feedback_correct: Correct! Trial sites have grown by 49% since 2019, contributing to the increased complexity of clinical trial management.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not the right figure. According to Slide 2, trial sites have grown by 49% since 2019, while protocol amendments have increased by 60%.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a module within the CTFS platform?
questions.feedback_correct: Right! Clinical data management is not part of CTFS. The platform focuses on financial modules like budgeting, contracting, forecasting, site payments, and participant payments.
questions.feedback_incorrect: That's actually part of CTFS. According to Slide 5, CTFS spans budgeting, contracting, forecasting, site payments, participant payments, and exception management—but not clinical data management.

questions.question: What is the estimated cost of delays in late-stage clinical trials per day, according to Applied Clinical Trials?
questions.feedback_correct: Correct! Late-stage trial delays can cost as much as $55,000 per day, making financial inefficiency a critical concern for trial execution.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Slide 3 cites Applied Clinical Trials' estimate that delays in late-stage trials can cost up to $55,000 per day, highlighting why financial efficiency matters.

questions.question: How many countries does CTFS support for participant payments?
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly! CTFS supports participant payments across more than 180 countries, making it truly global by design.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. While CTFS is supported across 200+ geographies, participant payment capabilities specifically extend to more than 180 countries, as noted on Slide 10.

questions.question: What architectural approach does CTFS use to support integration with external systems and future AI agents?
choices: Manual data transfer between isolated modules
questions.feedback_correct: Correct! CTFS uses a cloud-native, API-first design that supports integration through APIs and webhooks, allowing future capabilities to be connected without rebuilding the platform.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Slide 12 explains that CTFS is cloud-native and API-first, using APIs and webhooks to connect with EDC, CTMS, ERP systems, and future AI agents.

questions.question: According to the course, what is the projected reduction in financial processing time that customers may achieve with CTFS?
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly! Customer outcomes include a projected reduction of up to 50% in financial processing time through AI-powered automation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not the right percentage. Slide 11 indicates that CTFS can deliver up to 50% faster financial processing as a key customer outcome.

questions.question: What is described as the central problem that fragmented financial processes create for clinical trials?
choices: They increase the cost of software licensing
They limit visibility, increase errors and disputes, and consume time on administrative issues instead of trial advancement
They make it impossible to track budgets
They prevent sites from receiving payments
questions.feedback_correct: Excellent! Slide 3 explains that fragmented processes cause re-entry errors, limited visibility, disputes, and missed milestones because staff spend time on administrative tasks instead of advancing the trial.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The core problem described in Slide 3 is that fragmented financial processes limit visibility across sponsor and site, increase errors and disputes, and consume time on administrative work that could be spent advancing the trial.

questions.question: How does CTFS recommend approaching implementation to scale the platform across an organization?
choices: Deploy all CTFS capabilities simultaneously across the entire enterprise
Start with a large-scale transformation involving all financial workflows at once
Begin with a focused pilot on a measurable business problem and expand modularly as needs evolve
Implement only site payments and never add additional modules
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly! Slide 16 recommends launching a focused pilot tied to a measurable business problem, then measuring improvements before scaling—this is a pragmatic, modular approach.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Slides 13 and 16 emphasize a modular, phased approach: start with a focused pilot on a specific business problem, measure results, and expand across workflows—not an all-at-once enterprise deployment.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how CTFS orchestrates financial workflows compared to traditional approaches?
choices: It replaces all human decision-making with fully automated processes
It shifts from manual task completion to extracting information, validating against agreements, detecting anomalies, and intelligently routing items for human review
It eliminates the need for contract management entirely
It removes the need for any third-party integrations or external systems
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect! Slide 6 describes the shift from manual workflows to orchestration: information is extracted, validated, anomalies detected, and intelligently routed—focusing human attention on exceptions and decisions that require expertise.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Slide 6 explains that CTFS doesn't remove oversight; it refocuses human effort by orchestrating document ingestion, extraction, validation, anomaly detection, and intelligent routing so experts handle exceptions and decisions—not routine data handling.
